This paper establishes that for any two minimal actions of an infinite compact Hausdorff space by a finite group, which are continuously orbit equivalent, their associated reduced $C^*$-algebras are isomorphic precisely when their respective Bratteli diagrams are isomorphic. This result demonstrates a form of rigidity regarding continuous orbital equivalence in the context of finite group actions. The argument extends to show similar rigidity for actions involving virtually cyclic groups, covering both finite and infinite groups containing exactly one conjugacy class of maximal subgroups.

This work presents a nonparametric technique for estimating the conditional expectation operator $P_{X|Y}$ within the space of square-integrable functions on a domain $Y \subset \mathbb{R}^d$. The approach utilizes a sequence of finite-dimensional subspaces to approximate the operator via matrix operations. We establish that the resulting estimator is consistent and derive an upper bound for its mean integrated squared error (MISE). Furthermore, we demonstrate that the MISE lower bound is of the same order, confirming optimality. The estimator's performance is evaluated through simulations, and its application is illustrated using data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 to investigate the impact of education on earnings.

This study addresses the challenge of modeling epidemics using a continuous-time Markov chain framework, where the unobserved state vector represents the count of individuals in various health categories. The primary objective is to construct a reduced-order observer that accurately estimates the unobserved portion of this state, given only partial observations of a specific state component. This objective is achieved by formulating an optimization problem to determine the observer's gain matrix, which is then solved via a semidefinite programming approach. The practical utility and effectiveness of this observer design are demonstrated through a numerical example involving an SEIR epidemic model.

Knowledge graphs (KGs) are increasingly utilized to model real-world entities and their interrelations. While static KG models have achieved significant success in representing these structures, incorporating temporal information remains a challenge. This study addresses the challenge of link prediction within temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs). We introduce a novel methodology that adapts static link prediction models for use with TKGs. By reusing established static representations, our approach facilitates the training of TKG models with fewer parameters, resulting in improved performance. We validate this method across various TKG benchmarks, demonstrating that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Ultrashort pulse lasers operating in the near-infrared spectrum have become essential tools for advancing science and technology. Mode-locking techniques, particularly Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLML), are widely employed to generate pulses with high peak power. This study presents a comprehensive geometrical analysis of KLML, utilizing ABCD matrices to model the intracavity beam propagation. By accounting for the nonlinear focusing effect of the Kerr lens, we derived an analytical formula for the intracavity beam waist. This approach offers a practical method for optimizing KLML configurations, which is critical for achieving the highest possible peak power in oscillators. The derived beam-waist equation was validated through numerical simulations and compared against results from other analytical models. Furthermore, we examined the impact of the Kerr-lens aperture on the stability region of KLML oscillators. Our findings indicate that increasing the aperture size expands this stability region, thereby enabling the operation at higher intracavity powers.

Asynchronous online federated learning (AOL) is a distributed optimization technique designed to handle massive-scale online learning tasks. In this framework, clients process data streams locally and transmit their updates to a central server, which aggregates them to refine the global model. While AOL offers significant advantages over synchronous approaches by reducing waiting times and communication overhead, it introduces challenges related to communication heterogeneity and resource constraints. To address these issues, this paper introduces a new method tailored for nonlinear regression that explicitly accounts for clients' computational power and communication bandwidth. By enabling clients with limited resources to delay their transmission until a specific condition is met, the proposed approach ensures that all sent updates are valid, thereby enhancing the quality of the global model. Furthermore, the authors provide theoretical convergence guarantees for this resource-aware strategy and validate its effectiveness through extensive experiments.

This study evaluates the light absorption capabilities of silicon films integrated with various back reflectors, specifically comparing two-dimensional (2D) photonic crystal structures, three-dimensional (3D) photonic band gap (PBG) back reflectors, and standard Bragg mirrors. The 3D PBG design, constructed from a silicon-on-insulator substrate, functions as an efficient back reflector by suppressing light propagation in all directions. The findings indicate that the 3D PBG back reflector achieves superior performance compared to both 2D photonic crystals and conventional Bragg mirrors. This enhanced performance is particularly notable for ultrathin silicon layers, where the 3D structure enables absorption levels comparable to those of standard solar cells.

This work introduces a new asymptotic series for the solution to the infinite power tower equation, $x^x = z$. While the paper does not focus on tetration, defined as $^yx = x$, its findings offer valuable insights into the behavior of tetration. We establish that the solution $x$ can be expressed as a power series in $\ln(z)$, with coefficients determined recursively. The validity of this series is supported by numerical evidence, and we derive an asymptotic expansion for the principal real-valued solution, which converges for $z > e^{e/2}$. Furthermore, we examine the solution's dependence on $z$ within the complex plane, providing an asymptotic approximation for the count of complex solutions as $z \to \infty$.

We introduce a novel construction for high-dimensional expanders (HDXs) derived from finite group covers. Specifically, given a regular graph $G$ and a finite group $G$, we construct an HDX by taking the Cayley complex of a group $F$ acting on $G$ and taking the associated complex to be the universal cover of the graph $G$ times $F$. This construction yields the first infinite families of HDXs with linear spectral gap and linear isoperimetric gap for graphs that are not Ramanujan. Additionally, we establish a new link between the spectral gap and the existence of a large girth in the underlying graph, thereby creating the first infinite family of HDXs based on sparse graphs. This approach also provides the first infinite family of HDXs based on sparse graphs.

Gadolinium indium oxide (GdInO$_3$) is a quasi-two-dimensional honeycomb lattice antiferromagnet that exhibits a Néel transition at $T_N = 1.5$ K. This study investigates its magnetic behavior through temperature- and field-dependent magnetization, as well as specific heat measurements. The data reveal a significant enhancement in the magnetic moment at the Néel temperature, which is attributed to the presence of weakly coupled ferromagnetic correlations. Furthermore, the specific heat analysis indicates that the magnetic excitations are governed by a low-energy spin-wave spectrum.

Link prediction is a critical task in graph analysis, particularly for sparse networks where edges are scarce. Existing methods often fail to adequately capture the structural characteristics of these networks, resulting in suboptimal link prediction performance. To address this, we introduce Sparse Sparse Network Embedding (SSNE), a novel approach that generates effective node representations by integrating both local and global topological information. Specifically, we employ a two-stage process: initially, we derive a node-level embedding using the GraphSAGE framework, which captures local neighborhood patterns. Subsequently, we construct an edge-level embedding by aggregating the individual node representations. By jointly optimizing these representations based on global network topology, we generate the final sparse network embedding. Experimental results across multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in terms of link prediction accuracy.

We introduce an innovative approach to fabricating atomic vapor cells utilizing deep silicon micromachining. This method allows for the creation of a 2 cm long cell with a 2 mm diameter, featuring a 100 µm diameter optical window. The window is integrated into the cell body as a single piece of silicon, bonded via a 20 µm thick silicon oxide layer. This design enables the construction of complex internal geometries, such as a 2 mm diameter capillary tube, which facilitates the introduction of alkali metals. The resulting silicon cell exhibits superior mechanical and thermal properties compared to traditional glass versions. Additionally, the device is compatible with 3D printing techniques, allowing for the rapid production of custom-shaped housings. The fabricated silicon cell was tested using an optical pumping magnetometer, yielding a magnetic sensitivity of 100 fT/√Hz at 100 Hz.

This paper introduces a new model for nonlinear interference (NLI) power in dual-polarization formats, utilizing a novel approach to calculate cross-NLI contributions. The proposed model achieves a maximum NLI power estimation error of less than 1 dB across all dual-polarization configurations, outperforming the conventional Gaussian Noise model. The model's accuracy is validated through simulations of various dual-polarization transmission systems.

Detecting wildfires using remote sensing is a critical task for fire management, yet it remains difficult due to the sporadic nature of fires and the challenges in distinguishing them from other objects. While visible light imagery offers high detail, infrared (IR) images excel at revealing thermal signatures. This study introduces FIRe-GAN, a novel deep learning-based, unsupervised fusion method that leverages Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to integrate visible and infrared data. The proposed approach utilizes a two-stage training process: first, it trains a two-class classifier on visible images to generate synthetic labels for unsupervised learning; second, it trains a three-class discriminator to distinguish between fire, non-fire, and synthetic classes. The model's effectiveness was validated on a dataset comprising visible and IR images from the 2020 California wildfires, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods.

This study introduces a novel dataset designed for identifying indicators of depression within social media content. Developed through a rigorous process involving the systematic collection of postings, expert annotation by mental health professionals, and validation by a clinical psychologist, the dataset comprises 1,000 entries. It uniquely incorporates a multi-faceted evaluation framework that assesses posts across five distinct dimensions: suicidal ideation, anxiety, depression, cognitive dysfunction, and behavioral changes. This approach offers a significant advantage over prior research, which has primarily relied on single-label categorization. To validate the utility of this dataset, we conducted an empirical analysis using a state-of-the-art deep learning model based on bidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) networks. Our findings demonstrate that the multi-label classification strategy employed is both feasible and effective.

This study introduces a stochastic version of a compartmental model for COVID-19, extending the established SEIR framework by incorporating random variations into the system's differential equations. The analysis examines both the model's behavior under large and small random perturbations. Specifically, it investigates the ergodic properties of the resulting stochastic SEIR system and constructs an approximate, reduced-order stochastic SEIR model.

This study investigates the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance (ISGMR) in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si using inelastic scattering of $^{12}$C ions, a process that induces significant isoscalar monopole (ISGMR) and quadrupole (ISGQR) excitations. The experimental findings are analyzed using a theoretical framework based on the quasiparticle random phase approximation (QRPA), which incorporates an explicit coupling between the ISGMR and ISGQR. The analysis reveals that this coupling substantially influences the ISGMR characteristics, resulting in a notable reduction of the ISGQR energy centroid. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that accounting for this coupling is essential for accurately reproducing the ISGMR properties in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si.

This study examines friction-controlled dynamical systems, where the force of friction is modeled as the sum of a velocity-proportional viscous term and a constant dry friction term. The friction coefficient undergoes a discontinuous jump whenever the system's velocity reaches zero, a mechanism designed to induce velocity reversal. The primary objective is to analyze the convergence of these controlled systems toward the origin. The work begins by establishing the existence and uniqueness of solutions, which are proven to be differentiable almost everywhere. The analysis demonstrates that the convergence behavior is dictated by the specific control law employed. The study focuses on two scenarios: one involving a control law that is Lipschitz continuous, and another that is discontinuous. The findings indicate that both types of controllers can yield solutions that either exhibit stick-slip oscillations or converge to the origin. The paper further establishes sufficient criteria to determine which outcome—oscillation or convergence—will occur. The theoretical results are illustrated through examples of a feedback-controlled mass-spring-damper system and a feedback-controlled rigid body rotating about a fixed point.

This paper introduces a deep learning framework for solving the Bellman hedging problem, a critical component of model-free reinforcement learning. The approach represents the high-dimensional state-action space as a graph, where nodes signify states and edges signify actions. By applying a graph neural network to this structure, the method generates a policy that maximizes the estimated action values. The study demonstrates that the proposed deep learning architecture is mathematically equivalent to a message-passing reinforcement learning algorithm. Furthermore, the work establishes a connection between this framework and graph attention networks, offering a new perspective on attention mechanisms within reinforcement learning.

Sequential models have become a standard in e-commerce for generating item recommendations by capturing user behavior patterns. However, these models often overlook the specific intent behind a user's actions, which is crucial for effective recommendation. To address this gap, we introduce a novel approach that models the underlying intent of a user's actions. By utilizing a multi-task learning framework, our method simultaneously trains a sequential model for generating recommendations and an auxiliary model designed to capture user intent. This auxiliary model is trained on a binary classification task where the positive labels represent the next item a user actually selected, while the negative labels represent items not chosen. This setup allows the model to distinguish between relevant and irrelevant items, thereby encoding the user's intent. We demonstrate that incorporating this learned intent signal into the recommendation process significantly enhances performance. Empirical results across two real-world datasets confirm that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This work examines the reduction of the symmetric double confluent Heun equation to the reducible double conflutive Heun equation, a process that occurs when two of the three finite singularities merge into one. We demonstrate that the resulting equation possesses a specific set of characteristic exponents, which we utilize to establish a corresponding set of admissible monodromy matrices. Furthermore, we analyze the equation's behavior at infinity and derive the associated Stokes constants. Finally, we describe a symmetric deformation of the symmetric double conflutive Heun equation that features a singularity at the origin with a specific rank two Jordan block structure.

This study examines the recovery of a rank-one matrix from noisy observations, where the data is partitioned into groups, each containing multiple copies. Within every group, the signal-to-noise ratio remains constant but can fluctuate significantly between different groups. We establish information-theoretic lower bounds for the mean-squared error in estimating this matrix and identify the critical signal-to-noise threshold required for successful recovery. Our findings indicate that the mean-squared error is governed by the average groupwise signal-to-noise ratio, whereas the threshold depends on the most favorable (best) groupwise ratio. These results are applicable to diverse scenarios, including the estimation of latent factor loadings in fMRI studies, the identification of dominant components in climate data, and the analysis of gene expression profiles.

We introduce a topological framework for Weyl semimetals that does not depend on crystalline symmetry. By examining the Berry curvature of a generic three-dimensional Weyl Hamiltonian, we derive a set of topological invariants that characterize the system. These invariants dictate the core properties of the material, including the chiral anomaly, the Hall conductivity, and the degree of monopole charge associated with Weyl points. Crucially, unlike conventional models, our approach allows for a finite energy gap in the bulk spectrum, meaning the semimetallic state exists despite the absence of band crossings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the topological character of the system remains stable even when the bulk gap closes, provided the topological invariants are preserved.

We present a theoretical study of the lepton flavor universality ratio $R_{K}$ and $R_{K^{\prime}}$ within $b\to s\ell^+\ell^+$ transitions, utilizing a new effective Hamiltonian framework. This approach explicitly incorporates the Wilson coefficient $C_9^{\mu}$ alongside the entire set of Standard Model Wilson coefficients. By employing QCD factorization to address the hadronic matrix elements, we derive the total decay width, differential distributions, and the lepton flavor universality ratio $R_{K}$ for $B\to K^{(*)}\ell^+\ell^-$. Our findings indicate that the calculated $R_{K}$ and $R_{K^{\prime}}$ align with Standard Model predictions and are in agreement with current experimental data.

This work addresses the design of decentralized controllers for linear time-invariant systems with multiple inputs and outputs, where each local controller manages a specific input-output pair. The primary objective is to ensure that the global system achieves stability with every possible combination of local controllers. This property enables a "plug-and-play" capability, allowing new controllers to be added without destabilizing an already stable configuration. We present a method for creating such robustly stabilizing decentralized controllers by utilizing a frequency-domain approach grounded in H∞ control. This approach is applicable to a broad spectrum of systems, including those that are non-stabilizable or unstabilizable, and possess unstable modes located on the imaginary axis. Furthermore, we derive an algorithm to determine the maximum stability radius for a given multi-channel system, quantifying the largest allowable magnitude of unstable eigenvalues to maintain overall stability.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused a global crisis, resulting in significant loss of life and economic instability. As the number of confirmed cases rises, there is an urgent need for rapid and precise diagnosis to mitigate the spread of the virus. While traditional methods like RT-PCR remain the gold standard, they often suffer from delays and high costs. Consequently, this study introduces a novel, cost-effective diagnostic framework leveraging deep learning to analyze chest X-rays. The proposed system utilizes a two-stage approach: first, a pre-trained BERT model extracts features from the images, and second, a binary classifier distinguishes between healthy and COVID-19 patients. The findings indicate that this method achieves a high accuracy rate of 96.2%, demonstrating its potential as a reliable tool for identifying infected individuals.

Network analysis has become a vital tool for researchers across numerous disciplines, yet the field lacks a comprehensive, unified resource. This gap exists because existing literature is fragmented across various publications, each tailored to specific domains or audiences. To address this, we introduce "The Atlas of Network Science Methods," a book that consolidates hundreds of techniques from across disciplines into a single volume. This work is designed to be both a practical guide for experienced practitioners and an accessible entry point for students and early-career researchers. We believe this resource will significantly benefit aspiring network scientists by clarifying methodological choices and guiding them toward optimal decisions for their specific research contexts.

The field of eco-evolutionary dynamics has recently expanded significantly, driven by the integration of evolutionary processes into ecological models. This synthesis has been facilitated by rapid evolution, which occurs over timescales comparable to ecological fluctuations, and the concurrent development of theoretical frameworks and empirical methods for studying it. However, the relationship between ecological and evolutionary changes extends far beyond these short-term scenarios, spanning a vast spectrum from immediate behavioral adjustments to contemporary dynamics, and ultimately to the profound shifts characteristic of deep time. This review examines the connections between ecology and evolution across all these temporal scales, with a particular focus on the critical role of timescales. We explore how the speed of evolutionary processes influences ecological outcomes and how the magnitude of ecological changes feeds back to drive evolutionary trajectories. Furthermore, we analyze the mechanisms that alter timescales, including standing genetic variation, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation in polygenic traits, standing variation

Speech self-supervised learning (SSL) has recently emerged as a powerful method for extracting speech representations, with its efficacy in various downstream applications well-documented. However, the extent to which these models are susceptible to adversarial attacks remains largely unexplored. This study investigates the adversarial robustness of speech SSL, revealing that while these models are more resilient to white-box attacks compared to their performance in such scenarios, they remain significantly vulnerable in black-box settings. We attribute this disparity to the reliance of these systems on unlabeled data, which inadvertently leaks information about the training loss landscape, thereby facilitating effective attacks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that SSL-trained models can be successfully attacked using generated adversarial examples crafted against other SSL models, even those trained on different datasets. Finally, we explore strategies to mitigate these vulnerabilities, including the use of data augmentation and adversarial training, both of which have been shown to enhance robustness.

The decentralized finance (DeFi) sector has rapidly expanded, with blockchain-enabled decentralized exchanges (DEXs) serving as a primary component. This study examines the factors driving DEX adoption by analyzing data from the top 10 DEXs. Utilizing the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the research investigates how perceived ease of use, usefulness, and trust influence adoption rates. The findings indicate that both perceived usefulness and trust are significant determinants, whereas perceived ease of use is not. Additionally, the study reveals a positive correlation between the number of daily active users and trading volume, suggesting that traders are willing to sacrifice ease of use for greater perceived utility.

Sensitivity analysis is essential for drawing reliable conclusions from studies involving missing data, yet it often proves difficult to execute. This paper introduces a novel framework for conducting such analyses by employing the E-value, a metric representing the strength of unmeasured confounding. We outline a Bayesian approach to sensitivity analysis that leverages this concept, allowing researchers to define a credible interval for the E-value and subsequently estimate parameters conditional on these bounds. We demonstrate this method using two distinct Bayesian models: one utilizing a standard prior for the confounding strength E, and another employing a posterior distribution derived from observed data. Furthermore, we illustrate how to apply these sensitivity intervals to constrain effect size estimates and discuss the broader applicability of this approach to other statistical models.

This paper presents a comprehensive classification of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries defined on the Laurent extension of the quantum plane. We establish that the Drinfeld double of the group $D_2(q)$ serves as the symmetry Hopf algebra for the Laurent quantum plane, extending previously known $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-actions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Drinfeld double of the semi-direct product $S_2 \ltimes D_2(q)$ is the symmetry Hopf algebra for the Laurent quantum plane when the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-action is considered up to a gauge transformation.

The rapid proliferation of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) has created a significant demand for data, yet privacy concerns and data silos hinder the full exploitation of this data. Federated Learning (FL) offers a viable solution by enabling local model training on data that remains at the source, thereby mitigating privacy risks. However, FL struggles with the high latency and limited bandwidth typical of vehicular networks. Blockchain presents a promising alternative by ensuring data integrity, transparency, and security. This paper presents a systematic review of blockchain-enabled federated learning frameworks within the IoV domain. It outlines the advantages of integrating these technologies, identifies critical research challenges, and structures the analysis using the PRISM guidelines. Furthermore, it offers a comprehensive overview of existing FL applications in IoV and highlights the potential of combining FL with blockchain to address current limitations.

This study presents measurements of non-prompt and prompt D-meson production in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, utilizing data from the LHCb experiment. Non-prompt D-mesons are identified through their decays into final states containing an electron or muon from the subsequent bottom-hadron decay, while prompt D-mesons are reconstructed in both electron and hadronic final states. These measurements cover the rapidity interval $0 < y < 3.2$ and transverse momentum range $1 < p_{\rm T} < 32$ GeV/$c$. The results are expressed as differential cross-sections as functions of $p_{\rm T}$ and $y$, and are compared with predictions from various Monte Carlo simulations.

The Fermilab Large Cryogenic Facility (LCF) is being developed to support the construction of a large-scale quantum computing system. This initiative aims to create a centralized, millikelvin environment capable of housing hundreds of superconducting quantum processors. The LCF will feature a main dilution refrigerator operating at approximately 10 mK, complemented by a secondary system at 100 mK designed to manage ancillary components like control wiring, shielding, and cooling systems. Construction is expected to be completed in 2023, with the facility scheduled to become operational in 2024.

This paper presents a thorough analysis of crypto-related vulnerabilities found in open-source Python projects. By examining 10,000 PyPI packages containing 1.1 million lines of code, we identified 100 projects utilizing cryptography libraries and scrutinized their code for misuse. Our findings reveal that 16% of these projects contain at least one instance of crypto-related issues. The most prevalent problems include weak random number generation (36%), weak encryption algorithms (26%), and improper use of modes of operation (20%). Additionally, we observed that many developers fail to employ recommended libraries, such as the `hashlib` module for hashing, and that these issues are disproportionately common in smaller projects.

This paper introduces a straightforward yet highly effective method for automatic labeling in urban environments, leveraging extensive datasets. The proposed approach utilizes a voting system to determine the most probable class for an object by aggregating predictions from multiple models. Its primary advantage lies in the ability to parallelize computations across different models, thereby enhancing both accuracy and training speed. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through experiments on Cityscapes and BDD100K, where it achieves state-of-the-art results using only a fraction of the training data compared to existing methods.

This paper introduces a seismic reflectivity inversion method grounded in a nonuniform sparse model. We propose a new regularized inversion framework utilizing a nonuniform sparse prior, which is defined as a weighted combination of two functions: a soft thresholding operator and a smooth operator. The weight function varies spatially, being near zero at locations corresponding to reflectivity interfaces and approaching one elsewhere. This approach is designed to simultaneously capture sharp reflectivity boundaries and maintain smooth geological structures. We derive the gradient of the regularized cost function and develop an efficient inversion algorithm based on proximal averaging. Experimental results on both synthetic and real data demonstrate that the proposed method effectively generates high-fidelity synthetic realizations and accurate estimates of subsurface reflectivity.

This paper investigates the semigroups generated by composition operators on the space BMOA, specifically within the context of a general domain $D \subset \mathbb{C}$ that is simply connected and non-polar. The study focuses on characterizing the growth rates of these semigroups, which are determined by the underlying generator $\phi$. The analysis reveals that the growth is classified into three distinct categories: polynomial, exponential, or sub-exponential. For each category, the work provides characterizations of the corresponding generator $\phi$ and establishes links between these generators and specific subspaces of the space BMOA.

We investigate the finite-size scaling of the overlap between the ground state and a single excited state within the transfer-matrix framework. By analyzing this relationship, we demonstrate how to derive the fusion rules governing anyonic excitations. Furthermore, we establish a method for calculating the conformal dimensions of excited states using the scaling of the ground state overlap, a technique that has been validated against two distinct models. The first case involves the toric code, where we confirm the expected conformal dimensions for both Abelian and non-Abelian excitations. The second case examines the Haagerup model, allowing us to determine the conformal dimensions of its excitations and thereby constrain the structure of its anyon fusion ring.

This paper introduces a novel, robust part-of-speech (PoS) tagger designed for historical texts, utilizing a set-valued prediction framework. Rather than committing to a single tag for each word, the model generates a set of the most probable options, thereby mitigating errors associated with ambiguous classifications. This approach is particularly advantageous for PoS tagging, where a single misclassification can trigger downstream errors in morphological analysis. The study evaluates the model's efficacy on both contemporary and historical datasets, demonstrating that the set-valued method yields more dependable results than single-label alternatives. The model's architecture relies on a Conditional Random Field (CRF) enhanced with a set-valued decoding strategy, which simultaneously maximizes the likelihood of the predicted tag sets and minimizes their overlap. The proposed method is assessed using both a standard single-error rate metric and a newly defined set-overlap-based measure. The results indicate that the set-valued CRF not only achieves superior performance in terms of single-error rates but also generates significantly larger and more accurate tag sets compared to a single-label CRF. The implementation, available at https://github.com/roberts1999/savvy, is open-source.

This work introduces a new integrability theory designed for vector measures that accommodates a broader class of functions than previously possible. By utilizing a specific subclass of functions that includes all functions possessing finite non-decreasing oscillation, the theory extends beyond standard smooth assumptions. Consequently, it encompasses functions that are merely Riemann-Stieltjes integrable with respect to non-decreasing measures, as well as those with bounded variation under more general conditions. The framework also covers a wider variety of Lebesgue-integrable functions than the classic theory, specifically by incorporating functions with specific singularities. Furthermore, the approach simplifies the derivation of many fundamental results in analysis by eliminating the need for excessive smoothness conditions. A key advantage is that it eliminates reliance on the difficult-to-prove Denjoy-Carathéodory theorem, which is traditionally required to establish that every function of bounded non-decreasing oscillation admits an integral representation. By bypassing this complex requirement, the new theory streamlines proofs for many essential analytical properties.

We introduce a formal specification assistant that leverages intelligent techniques to aid software engineers in translating user requirements into formal specifications. This tool supports the step-by-step derivation of specifications from requirements, utilizing an intelligent agent to recommend next actions based on the current state. The agent employs a reasoning mechanism to navigate a state space, identifying the most effective transition at each step. The system's architecture is built upon an Interval Temporal Logic (ITL) specification language, which is paired with a tailored graph representation designed to facilitate automated reasoning. The proposed tool is implemented in Haskell and is available for use at https://github.com/eduardo-oliveira/requirement-specification-assistant.

Quantum error mitigation (QEM) is a vital strategy for near-term quantum devices, enabling the enhancement of noisy quantum circuit results. This work introduces a QEM approach tailored for open quantum systems that interact with their environment. The method relies on applying a concealed inverse operation to a circuit's noisy output, where this inversion is realized through a complementary interaction with the same environment. We demonstrate that this protocol effectively reverses the impact of arbitrary noise occurring within the circuit. Additionally, we show that the protocol can partially reverse environmental decoherence arising from photon loss. Finally, we provide an analysis of its resource requirements and performance, which we validate through experiments on a superconducting quantum processor.

In a regular category, the direct image of a preorder via a regular epimorphism generally fails to be a preorder; however, there exists a unique smallest such subrelation on the codomain known as the cocartesian image of that preorder. This paper establishes that this cocartesian image can be constructed as the image factorization of a specific span, where the span's source is the cocartesian product of the preorder with itself and the target map is the codiagonal. Dually, the cocartesian image of a preorder is characterized as the image factorization of a span involving the equivalence to a point (the diagonal) of that preorder as the target map, with the source map being a specific regular monomorphism. This morphism is the equalizer of a pair of maps defined on the product of the preorder with itself and its codiagonal, respectively. Furthermore, the cocartesian image of an equivalence relation within a regular category is demonstrated to be the image factorization of a span involving the domain of that relation as the target map, with the source map being the pullback of the original relation along a specific regular epimorphism.

This study introduces a novel framework for modeling multivariate conditional extremes, specifically addressing scenarios where multiple variables are constrained by several lower bounds. The work begins by defining the multivariate conditional distribution function and establishing the requisite properties for the resulting density function. The authors subsequently present a specific parametric model, demonstrating that the density can be expressed as a product of marginal densities and a structured copula density. The paper further derives the corresponding likelihood function and proposes an estimation method based on the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm. Finally, the utility of this approach is illustrated through an application focused on modeling extreme ocean conditions, utilizing real-world data collected from the North Sea.

Recent advancements in vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable efficacy in zero-shot image classification. However, these models typically rely on generic text prompts, which often lack the specific details necessary for precise classification. To address this limitation, we introduce VT-CLIP, a framework designed to generate specialized text descriptions for images to bolster zero-shot performance. Our approach features a novel Visual-Text Transformer (VT) module that produces refined image descriptions by leveraging visual features. These descriptions are then integrated with CLIP's textual encoder to create enhanced, visual-guided text prompts for classification. Empirical evaluations on zero-shot benchmarks, including ImageNet-1K and Concept12M, confirm that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art results.

We introduce a novel operator shifting framework designed to solve general noisy matrix equations of the form $AXB + C = E$, where $A$ and $B$ are invertible, and both the matrix $C$ and its solution $X$ are unknown. This work extends prior operator shifting methods, which were limited to the noiseless case $AXB = C$, by accommodating uncertainty in these terms. We present a general operator shifting strategy that enables the computation of approximations for $X$ using only a single matrix-vector multiplication with $C$. This approach leverages the polynomial root isolation properties of the underlying polynomials to achieve a convergence rate of $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ for an error tolerance $\varepsilon$. Furthermore, we establish a connection between our operator shifting method and the classical Chebyshev acceleration technique.

We demonstrate that the $n$-slice of the quaternionic Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectrum $\mathbb{H}X_n$ constitutes a ring spectrum whose homotopy groups form the graded algebra of polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_2$ with generators located in degrees $4k+1$ and $4k+2$ (for $k=0,\dots,n-1$) that are annihilated by the Milnor operations $Sq^2$ and $Sq^3$. Furthermore, we establish that this slicing is associative, commutative, and distributes over the lexicographic sum of polynomials.

This paper introduces the tight Hilbert polynomial, a new invariant for a local ring $R$ that measures the maximum number of elements contained in a tight closure of an ideal generated by $n$ elements within powers of that ideal. We demonstrate that for a parameter quasi-excellent domain $S$ of characteristic $p>0$ and a system of parameters $\boldsymbol{x}$, the localizations $S_{\boldsymbol{x}}$ are F-rational if and only if the corresponding tight Hilbert polynomial evaluated at $\boldsymbol{x}$ equals the integer $p^n$. Additionally, we provide examples illustrating the significance of this polynomial in determining the structure of F-rational rings.

Digital pathology and radiology are increasingly leveraging machine learning for tasks such as cell counting, tumor segmentation, and lesion detection. However, a significant hurdle remains the lack of unified standards for sharing these model outputs, which impedes reproducibility and collaboration. To address this, we introduce Highdicom, a Python library that encapsulates DICOM standards specifically for secondary capture data, including annotations and model predictions. Highdicom offers tools to create, validate, and parse these objects, ensuring they adhere strictly to protocol specifications. By facilitating the exchange of results in a compliant format, the library supports enhanced collaboration and experimental verification within the field.

This work examines the boundary contribution within the Einstein-Hilbert action, deriving its Noether current and associated charges. We demonstrate that the algebra formed by these specific charges at the boundary is isomorphic to the Virasoro algebra. Furthermore, we establish that the entropy of the AdS black hole can be expressed as the null charge of a corresponding Killing vector field.

Deep learning has recently become a powerful tool for extracting DNA representations, yet most existing models rely on labeled data and are often overfitted. This study introduces an unsupervised approach that learns DNA representations by modeling sequences as graphs and applying graph convolutional networks. We evaluate this method on three distinct tasks: sequence classification, motif discovery, and binding site prediction. Our results indicate that the representations generated by this unsupervised framework are highly competitive with those produced by supervised models, while also demonstrating greater generalization capabilities.

The metal-insulator transition (MIT) in vanadium dioxide (V$_2$O$_3$) is a highly debated topic, with recent studies on V$_2$O$_3$ ultrathin films (ULFs) suggesting that the MIT is governed by surface termination. To validate this hypothesis, we conducted a systematic investigation of the MIT in V$_2$O$_3$ ULFs grown on SrTiO$_3$ substrates, utilizing temperature-dependent transport measurements and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). Our results indicate that the MIT is not solely dictated by surface termination but is instead a combined effect of both terminations. Specifically, the (0001)A-terminated surface exhibits a clear MIT, whereas the (0001)B-terminated surface displays insulating behavior. Furthermore, we observed that the thickness of the insulating B-terminated layer influences the overall MIT characteristics of the film.

The canonical forms established by the Bohnenblust, Grothendieck, and Sobolev for Lie-Poisson systems are derived through a method that extends the classical technique of the Grothendieck and the Birkhoff. This method relies on the action of the group of Lie-Poisson transformations on a Lie-Poisson system's potential function, utilizing the associated moment map. This function serves as the solution to a Lie-Poisson equation where the right-hand side is a linear Poisson cocycle. Furthermore, the paper presents a procedure for the normalization of Lie-Poisson potentials, a process that enables the attainment of the aforementioned canonical forms.

The Kepler Transiting NET (KMT) has identified numerous exoplanets, including several with highly eccentric orbits. This study presents a systematic search for exoplanets with eccentricities exceeding 0.3 within the KMTNet sample of transit anomalies observed during 2018. The analysis covers the 2018 dataset, which includes 2,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,00

In this paper, we investigate the influence of adding dissipation terms to a broad category of hyperbolic conservation laws. We demonstrate that for any initial data within a sufficiently large $L^{\infty}$ ball, global weak solutions exist for the viscous form of the conservation law, where the viscosity is governed by a smooth, positive coefficient function dependent on the state variables. Furthermore, we establish that these conservation laws are strictly controlled in the sense that the corresponding semigroup remains uniformly bounded in $L^{\infty}$ for all $t \geq 0$. As an application of these findings, we analyze the three-dimensional compressible barotropic Navier-Stokes equations, proving the existence of global weak solutions for any initial data within a fixed $L^{\infty}$ ball. Additionally, we show that these solutions are uniformly bounded in $L^{\infty}$ over time, and we derive a new a priori estimate for the $H^{1}$ norm of the velocity field.

This study introduces a novel approach to analyzing feature importance within machine learning models by leveraging the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) framework. Using a Non-Performing Loan (NPL) dataset, the research evaluates multiple algorithms—including Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and Logistic Regression—across various performance metrics. The analysis focuses on two distinct data subsets: one comprising only loans with complete information and another including records with missing values. The findings indicate that the XGBoost model achieves the highest performance on the subset with complete data, while LightGBM excels on the subset containing missing values. Additionally, the paper examines how the number of trees in an XGBoost model influences both model performance and the calculated Shapley values.

A Dyck path is a lattice trajectory from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ that remains above the diagonal. Its associated Dyck path graph is constructed using lattice points above the diagonal as vertices, with edges connecting points that share a row or column. This work presents a combinatorial formula for the chromatic symmetric function of these objects, derived through a novel application of $q$-rook theory. As a consequence, we establish an extended version of the Lindstr\"{o}m-Gessel-Viennot lemma applicable to lattice paths in the first quadrant.

We introduce a novel convolutional network architecture that leverages orientation-based kernels to achieve superior performance on the ImageNet dataset. This design is a streamlined adaptation of the orientation convolutional layer proposed in \cite{orikon}, which utilizes orientation-specific filters and orientation-based pooling. By integrating orientation convolutions with orientation-aware residual blocks and an orientation-specific global average pooling layer, our model surpasses the state-of-the-art on the ImageNet-2012 validation set, reaching an accuracy of 82.6%.

We introduce a novel relative trace formula that evaluates linear periods on $GL_{2n}(F)$ twisted by the character $\det^{s}$, where $F$ denotes a local field. This formula is constructed by applying the relative trace formula method to a relative Langlands-Shahidi framework utilizing appropriate test functions.

The determination of the top quark mass within the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme relies on theoretical predictions that incorporate quantum corrections from lighter quarks. This study examines how such massive flavors influence the renormalization group evolution of the top quark mass, specifically analyzing the $\mu$-dependence of the associated matching coefficient. By employing an expansion in powers of the lighter quark mass divided by the top quark mass, we evaluate the $\mu$-dependence arising from the leading term of this series. Our findings indicate that, for the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ mass, the residual $\mu$-dependence of the leading term is negligible across the standard range of renormalization scales. Consequently, the $\mu$-dependence observed in the $\mu$-$\mu$-dependence of the leading term of the $\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$\mu$-$

This paper addresses the sequential edge-coloring problem on a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, where edges are revealed one by one in a predetermined order, requiring an online algorithm to assign colors adaptively. The objective is to minimize the total number of colors used. We establish a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1/2})$ for regular graphs and a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{1/2}(\log n)^{1/2})$ for graphs with degree at most $n^{1/4}$. Additionally, we present an efficient algorithm capable of achieving a competitive ratio of $O(n^{1/4})$ for any graph.

This paper introduces several hypercontractive inequalities relating to weighted Bergman spaces. We establish an operator version of a hypercontractive inequality for the weight function $e^{-|x|^2}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, which is instrumental in addressing the discrete setting. Additionally, we formulate and prove a discrete analogue of the continuous inequality previously stated.

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has caused a global crisis, resulting in over 10 million confirmed cases and more than 500,000 deaths. While RT-PCR remains the gold standard for detection, its limitations include high costs, lengthy processing times, and the need for specialized facilities. Consequently, there is an urgent demand for rapid, cost-effective, and accurate diagnostic methods. This study introduces a novel two-stage Time-distributed Capsule Network (TD-Cap) designed to identify COVID-19 from chest CT images. The first stage employs a 3D U-Net for feature extraction, while the second utilizes TD-Cap capsules to classify the input. The model is trained on 1,000 CT scans from the OUCU dataset, which includes 250 confirmed COVID-19 cases and 750 non-infected controls. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed TD-Cap network achieves a top-1 accuracy of 90.1% and a top-5 accuracy of 98.1%. These results surpass those of state-of-the-art methods, including ResNet5D (86.4% top-1), DenseNet121D (86.4% top-1), and a standard CNN (86.4% top-1), establishing the proposed architecture as a highly effective tool for automated diagnosis.

This paper introduces a methodology for modeling the stochastic distribution of active satellites within the low Earth orbit (LEO) space environment. The study derives the probability density function (PDF) for the number of satellites occupying a specific shell within a designated orbital plane and examines the statistical characteristics of space occupancy. The approach is applicable to scenarios involving both randomly and non-randomly distributed satellites across different orbital planes. The paper further investigates the implications of these findings for the risk of on-orbit collisions and the potential for spectrum interference.

In the field of computer graphics, quad meshing is highly favored over other methods because quads offer superior visual quality and greater flexibility for subsequent processing tasks. However, creating high-order coarse quads on CAD models remains a difficult challenge. This paper introduces a novel ILP-based technique for generating high-order coarse quad meshes on CAD models. The approach relies on defining a set of local constraints for each vertex and formulating a global ILP that optimizes these constraints. The resulting high-order coarse quads are then converted into fine quads using a new ILP-driven subdivision method. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through various examples.

This paper introduces formulas for the sample mean and sample variance of the sample correlation coefficient when calculated over all possible permutations of one dataset relative to a second. These moments are expressed as specific weighted sums of the sample correlations between every possible pair of subsets drawn from the combined pool of both datasets. The primary application of these results lies in developing a highly efficient algorithm to rapidly approximate the significance of a given sample correlation coefficient.

This study introduces a general methodology for deriving gravitational scattering amplitudes, grounded in the Einstein-Hilbert action and applicable to an arbitrary number of photons. The method's validity is confirmed by reproducing known results for graviton interactions in both de Sitter and anti-de Sitter spacetimes. The computational procedure involves two primary stages: first, constructing the on-shell three-point amplitude via the spinor-helicity formalism, and second, employing a bootstrap strategy to determine the full $S$-matrix by enforcing consistency with a specific set of physical principles.

This study examines the stabilization of the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations within critical $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces. By utilizing a finite-dimensional, fully localized interior feedback control, we establish the uniform stabilization of a given steady state. This result extends previous work by Fabre, Puel, and Tenenbaum, who addressed the homogeneous equations with zero boundary conditions, to the general case involving arbitrary data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the $L^q$-based Besov space $\mathcal{B}_{2,\infty}^{-2}$ serves as a critical space for this problem.

This paper introduces the LiTMind Dictionary, a newly developed, open-source online dictionary designed to support non-specialists and researchers in accessing definitions for classical Chinese texts. By integrating comprehensive text data, definitions, and cross-references, the tool facilitates efficient lookup of vocabulary within ancient literature. To enhance its utility, the system incorporates modern Chinese translations and links to parallel entries, enabling users to grasp word meanings through contextual comparison. Furthermore, the dictionary features an open architecture that allows for the seamless addition of new entries and the expansion of existing resources.

Explainable recommendation systems (RecSys) are increasingly vital for assisting users in making informed decisions. While Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Attribution (LIME) is a widely adopted method for generating local explanations, it has been observed to produce inconsistent results. This study introduces Adherence and Constancy as two new metrics for evaluating RecSys-specific LIME explanations, which are found to be independent of existing general LIME metrics. The authors demonstrate that adherence and constancy are positively correlated with each other and that adherence correlates with user satisfaction. Consequently, adherence is recommended as a key metric for assessing the quality of LIME explanations within the recommendation domain.

The electronic properties of semiconductor interfaces are governed by Fermi level pinning, a phenomenon where the interface state density dictates the position of the Fermi level. In this study, we examine the interface between InAs quantum wells and In$_{0.82}$Ga$_{0.18}$As barrier layers, which are grown on GaAs substrates. We demonstrate that the interface Fermi level can be manipulated by adjusting the density of interface defects. Furthermore, we show that the carrier density within the quantum well is highly sensitive to the interface Fermi level, a relationship that can be leveraged to create reconfigurable devices.

This paper investigates the utility of local queries for learning robustly within the PAC framework. We establish that for any query class $\mathcal{C}$ possessing finite VC dimension, there exists a local learning algorithm capable of achieving robust accuracy with probability 1 over samples. This algorithm's sample complexity is polynomial in the VC dimension of $\mathcal{C}$ and its local dimension, provided the robust error is sufficiently small. Conversely, we demonstrate that local queries offer no advantage for robust learning in scenarios where the target concept is inherently robust to a specific degree. We further present an algorithm that leverages local queries to achieve robust PAC learnability for a collection of concepts with finite local dimension and robustness radius. Finally, we provide a negative result indicating that local queries do not facilitate robust PAC learnability for an infinite family of concepts characterized by finite local dimension and robustness radius, yet possessing infinite VC dimension.

In this paper, we introduce an innovative algorithm for performing optimal transport between two $n$-dimensional discrete measures. This method leverages the specific structure of Sinkhorn's alternating scaling algorithm to achieve an exact solution in $O(n^2)$ time. We demonstrate that the algorithm's efficiency stems from the fact that the resulting optimal transport cost matrix exhibits a "collinear" property, meaning it can be effectively approximated by a sequence of small triangular matrices of size $O(\sqrt{n})$. We present the algorithm, provide a proof of its correctness, and evaluate its performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our results indicate that the method is highly competitive with state-of-the-art approaches, particularly excelling in scenarios involving large $n$ values.

This study presents the most extensive analysis of far-ultraviolet (FUV) emissions from the active M1 star AU Mic, utilizing data from the Swift UV/Optical Telescope Array (UVOT) and the International Space Station's Atmospheric Imaging Imager (ISSI). We report the detection of significant flares in the FUV band, with peak fluxes reaching approximately 100 times the quiescent level. These flares align with those observed in the optical spectrum, showing consistent durations and recurrence patterns. Furthermore, we identify a distinct "soft" component in the FUV flare emission that is notably weaker than the "hard" component, a feature that persists across both bands. During quiescent phases, the star's FUV spectrum exhibits a strong continuum alongside prominent emission lines from highly ionized species, including O VI, N V, and C IV. We estimate the total mass-loss rate for the system to be roughly $10^{13}$ g s$^{-1}$, a figure that exceeds previous optical and X-ray estimates by a factor of ten. Additionally, we calculate the XUV irradiance received by the exoplanets AU Mic b and c, finding that it surpasses the total stellar irradiation they receive by a similar order of magnitude. These findings underscore the profound impact stellar activity has on the atmospheric evolution of close-in exoplanets.

This work examines the impact of a medium's resistance on the motion of a charged particle, specifically analyzing how dissipative effects alter the standard Abraham-Lorentz-Dirac equation. We derive a modified equation incorporating this medium resistance and compare it against the conventional model. Furthermore, we investigate the implications for energy radiation within this context, demonstrating that the medium can significantly suppress radiative losses.

This study investigates the impact of data imbalance on nearest neighbor classification, specifically examining how the proportion of minority classes influences performance. We demonstrate that the probability of error in nearest neighbor classification can be expressed as a function of the ratio between majority and minority classes, alongside the distance between their respective class-conditional densities. Furthermore, we establish that this error probability is minimized when the classifier operates on data drawn from an optimal mixture of these densities. Finally, we propose a novel classification method that projects data points onto a transformed feature space designed to equalize class imbalances, thereby enhancing the accuracy of nearest neighbor classification.

We introduce a novel sample of 100 high-redshift quasars ($z > 2$) identified through photometric redshift estimation using SkyMapper data. These quaseries exhibit bolometric luminosities spanning from $10^{45}$ to $10^{48}$ erg s$^{-1}$, with a median value of $10^{47.2}$ erg s$^{-1}$. The distribution of their rest-frame UV magnitudes is notably broad, ranging from 18 to 30 mag. We cross-referenced our list with existing quasar catalogs, finding that 90% of the objects are new discoveries. By combining our findings with data from the literature, we derived a luminosity function for the range $10^{43} < L_{1450} < 10^{48}$ erg s$^{-1}$ across $2 < z < 5$. Our results indicate that the most luminous quaseries ($L > 10^{47}$ erg s$^{-1}$) are significantly more abundant at lower redshifts ($z < 3$) than at higher ones, a trend that aligns with the observed decline in the cosmic star formation rate density.

This study investigates the tunneling dynamics between a quantum dot and a superconducting island within a hybrid system. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the quantum dot's charge state can be detected through shifts in the superconducting island's resonance frequency. Our findings indicate that charge tunneling generates a non-zero average energy within the superconducting island, which is contingent on the presence of a finite tunneling amplitude and a non-zero average energy of the dot. Additionally, the amplitude of these frequency shifts is governed by the coupling strength between the dot and the island, as well as the occupation numbers of the quantum dot.

This work examines the contraction property of admissible discontinuities in hyperbolic conservation laws, utilizing $L^\infty$ metrics defined by convex entropies. A sufficient condition for contraction at such entropic discontinuities is derived, expressed in terms of the eigenvalues of the relaxation matrix and a specific matrix involving the eigenvectors and the entropy gradient. This condition applies to both shock and rarefaction discontinuities, with rarefactions requiring an additional constraint on the jump in the entropy gradient. The findings are illustrated through examples drawn from gas dynamics and traffic flow models.

We introduce DiffDreamer, a conditional diffusion framework designed to create an infinite sequence of novel views from a single input image. By leveraging pre-trained large-scale image-to-image models, the system synthesizes high-fidelity imagery for unseen camera angles while maintaining the integrity of the original scene's content. To ensure long-term consistency across these continuously generated views, we employ a two-stage strategy. First, we utilize a two-step parameter optimization approach to align the latent space of the base diffusion model with the space of generated images, thereby enhancing cross-stage feature alignment. Second, we develop a multi-step lookahead mechanism that projects future latent representations into the current latent space before decoding, which significantly improves view-to-view coherence. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our method surpasses existing techniques in both qualitative and quantitative metrics.

This work introduces a novel, entirely data-driven approach to modeling, analyzing, and controlling networked epidemic models. The core methodology involves constructing a linear state-space representation for a networked system by utilizing only partial observational data. This representation is subsequently employed to design a linear control strategy that ensures the containment of an emerging epidemic. The study demonstrates the efficacy of this proposed framework through a control-oriented analysis of networked Susceptible-Infected (SI) models. The authors validate their approach by applying it to a synthetic networked SIS model and by evaluating its performance against existing methods using real-world data from a networked SIS model.

The instability of a liquid film coating a solid cylinder is examined, with a specific focus on the influence of slip at the liquid-solid interface. The analysis begins by establishing the governing equations for a thin film in a moving coordinate system that translates at the instability's growth rate. Following this, the problem is solved using the method of matched asymptotic expansions, revealing that slip significantly accelerates the instability. This enhancement arises because slip generates a substantial radial flow within the thinning neck region, which counteracts surface tension forces. The findings from this theoretical model are compared against existing experimental data and numerical simulations, showing strong agreement.

This work establishes the Lipschitz stability of weak solutions for the Hunter-Saxton equation within the framework of measure-valued solutions. Building upon this result, we demonstrate the uniqueness of these measures weak solutions.

This study investigates the dependability of an automated, robot-guided ultrasound technique for measuring scoliosis curvature via ultrasound scanning (USS) when compared to traditional manual scanning. The research focuses on two critical factors: inter-scan consistency and the agreement between robotic and manual approaches. The results indicate that inter-scan reliability for both methods is high, with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) exceeding 0.80 for the maximum lateral curvature angle. Regarding the agreement between the two scanning techniques, a strong positive correlation was observed (r = 0.82), and paired t-tests revealed no statistically significant difference in the measured angles. However, the ICC between robotic and manual scans indicated moderate to good agreement, falling between 0.61 and 0.75. These findings suggest that robotic-assisted scanning is a dependable method for scoliosis assessment, demonstrating comparable performance to manual scanning in terms of both reliability and inter-method agreement.

This study introduces a new methodology for creating synthetic speech durations by leveraging a non-parametric approach. By calculating the median of real speech duration segments, the method avoids reliance on restrictive assumptions regarding the underlying statistical distribution. The study evaluates this technique against a standard Parametric Approach (PA), which models durations using a Gaussian distribution of mean and variance. The results demonstrate that the proposed Median-Based Approach (MBA) achieves superior performance over PA, particularly in handling outliers and modeling complex distributional characteristics.

In recent times, the use of social media platforms has surged, facilitating communication among individuals across the globe. However, this connectivity has also given rise to online hate speech, which poses significant challenges to society. This study introduces a novel method for identifying such content by leveraging a feature extraction approach. We developed a model that integrates multiple social media metrics with the Word2Vec technique to identify hate speech. Experimental results indicate that this model achieves an accuracy of 90.1%, an F1 score of 89.9%, and a recall rate of 90.0%.

This paper introduces a novel Multi-input Multi-output (MIMO) architecture designed to handle multiple feature maps simultaneously. By utilizing multiple feature maps, the approach enables the integration of diverse layers and facilitates the reuse of intermediate features. The architecture employs two primary mechanisms: first, it uses multiple feature maps to store and share features across different branches; second, it incorporates multiple outputs to execute feature fusion and feature extraction in parallel. The study presents a comprehensive analysis of the proposed architecture, including its design principles, implementation details, and performance evaluation. The results demonstrate that the proposed architecture achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, particularly in terms of computational efficiency and overall accuracy.

This paper provides a comprehensive survey of datasets for the domain of historical document image analysis. It begins by examining the challenges within this field, including the scarcity of annotated data, the complexity of document structures, and the need for specialized processing techniques. The study then presents a systematic classification of existing datasets according to their content, covering various writing systems, document types, and historical periods. Furthermore, the authors describe the associated processing pipelines for each collection, addressing tasks such as image enhancement, segmentation, and the generation of training data. The work concludes by outlining future research directions and potential applications for these resources.

This study introduces a flatness-based control strategy for an industrial robot joint equipped with a secondary encoder, designed to mitigate backlash and friction effects. The paper details the derivation of a dynamic model that incorporates backlash and friction, which is subsequently linearized via a flatness-based feedback control law. To enhance tracking accuracy, a second encoder is utilized to develop an observer capable of estimating the internal states of the robot joint. The proposed control architecture is validated through experimental results, which demonstrate a significant reduction in tracking error.

Chronic diseases, such as myocardial infarction (MI), are characterized by a complex trajectory involving multiple health states, including acute phases, chronic phases, and recurrent episodes. While survival analysis is commonly used to study these diseases, it is limited to examining only a single outcome. This study introduces multidimentional multiple time-to-event analysis (MME), a novel methodology that simultaneously models several time-to-event outcomes. We demonstrate that MME can effectively capture the full complexity of disease progression, using longitudinal MI data from the Cardiovascular Health Study to illustrate its application.

We introduce a quadrature scheme designed to calculate molecular collision integrals for the Boltzmann equation, featuring multiple centers for efficiency. This method employs a piecewise constant approximation of the Maxwellian distribution, which is then integrated exactly against the cross section. The selection of these centers is optimized to minimize quadrature error, with the overall error bounded by the maximum error within each piecewise interval. The proposed scheme is validated against benchmark results from the Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method, demonstrating that it achieves high accuracy with as few as 10 points per cell.

The metric dimension problem involves determining the smallest subset $S$ of a graph's vertices such that every other vertex possesses a distinct distance vector relative to this set. This study examines the complexity of parameterizing that problem using feedback vertex set and related structural metrics. We demonstrate that it is W[1]-hard when parameterized by the sum of ordered and unordered metric dimensions, by feedback edge set size, or by bounded-degree tree width. Conversely, we prove that the problem admits a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm when parameterized by tree width, and that it is both XP and W[1]-hard when parameterized by path vertex cover.

We establish that this monad is directed, meaning it preserves the subspaces and unions of directed sets.
